title: HTTPS, TLS & Certificates
oneLiner: Encryption is only half of HTTPS. The certificate is how your browser knows who's on the other end.
keyTakeaway: A certificate binds a site name to a public key (the shareable half of a key pair; only the holder of the matching private key can produce signatures it verifies), vouched for by a chain of signatures ending at a root your browser already trusts. The browser checks the chain, the dates and the name; if any check fails, the connection may be encrypted but you can't know who you're talking to -- so never train people to click through the warning.
explanation:
HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS. TLS does two jobs. It encrypts everything between browser and server so nobody in between (the coffee-shop Wi-Fi, a compromised router) can read or change it. And it authenticates the server, so you know the encrypted connection goes to the real academy.conperio.com and not an impostor. Encryption without that second part is a private conversation with a stranger. The DNS & HTTP lesson in Networking shows where the TLS handshake fits in loading a page.

The server proves its identity with a certificate: a small document saying "this public key belongs to academy.conperio.com, valid from this date to that one", signed by a certificate authority (CA). That CA's own certificate is signed by another, up to a root CA whose certificate ships with your operating system or browser. Following those signatures up to a trusted root is building the chain. Servers must send the intermediate certificates along with their own; forgetting to is a common misconfiguration that some browsers paper over and others don't.

The browser then checks three things, shown in the demo: the chain reaches a trusted root, every certificate is in date, and the certificate actually names the site in the address bar. A self-signed certificate fails the first check (anyone can sign their own), which is fine on a developer laptop and never fine in production. Companies often run their own internal CA and install its root on company machines, which makes internal certificates trusted on those machines only.

Certificates expire on purpose, now at most 200 days (falling to 47 days by 2029), and 90 days with Let's Encrypt, so automate renewal (Let's Encrypt with cert-manager in Kubernetes is the common setup). Expired certificates are one of the most common causes of outages that "nobody changed anything" before.
